title: The map under the turning bar
method: Turn the Map Room’s old counter sketch against the same landmarks.
request: Marek has one rolling frame and two crews. One stands at the canal gate and one at the map-room door. Their left and right start in different places.

views.label: Start from the canal gate
views.read: The gate starts at the bottom of the board. From it the landing is left of the store. The same bridge joins both banks.

views.label: Turn the board toward the map-room door
views.read: The landing is now right of the store from the opposite start. It is still the same landing. Al-Idrisi’s map puts south above north, with its own purpose and convention.

placements.label: Put both starting points on the handover board
placements.after: Marek keeps the same bridge line and pins a named start to either end. The arriving crew can turn the sheet before walking.

placements.label: Keep the bridge mark large and leave the frame free to turn
placements.after: The crew finds the familiar bridge on a quick pass. The keeper can rotate the work board within reach when someone comes from the other side.

question: When the same landmarks are seen from two doors, whose left and right should a map use?
journal: I turned the frame from the canal gate to the door. The landing changed sides on my sheet. The bridge kept both ends. I know which starting point to ask for next time someone says “left.”
firstHint: The canal gate and the door give two people different places to start the same walk.
thirdHint: Turn the frame at the door. Follow the bridge back both times.

title: The rehearsal board beside the record sleeves
method: Separate what a guide’s board shows from what its keeper can authorise.
request: The workroom’s new guide will use its own plain pegs to remember an invented handover. A visitor is asking for a transcription of the historical Luba lukasa.

views.label: Follow the workroom guide’s pegs
views.read: On this local practice board, the guide can tell who waited at the bench. Moving the pegs alone does not identify the people without the person’s account.

views.label: Open the named Brooklyn record
views.read: The accession gives a public account of the Luba object and the learning of Mbudye members. The display has no key for decoding its markings or authority to retell the knowledge they prompt.

placements.label: Lead with the guide and leave the catalogue within reach
placements.after: The workroom offers the live local example with the Brooklyn record on a separately named leaf. The guide answers for the example they actually made.

placements.label: Leave the public record first and put the exercise on the side bench
placements.after: The visitor can begin at the Brooklyn accession. The practice board stays visibly separate beside the workroom guide’s table.

question: What can a guide's board show, and what can only its keeper decide?
journal: I could move every peg on the guide’s practice board. I still had to ask who had waited at the bench. The Brooklyn record gave me an accession to share. It could never give me a Mbudye interpreter’s part.
firstHint: The guide knows who waited. A visitor looking only at the practice pegs has a different view.
thirdHint: Hear what the workroom guide can tell from the local exercise. Open the museum record for what the public caption actually supports.

title: The harbour watch with a narrow window
method: Test how the width of a lookout window changes a claim about what crossed.
request: Ruan has found a second watch slip. Its observer used the narrow opening. One boat track passed the outer frame.

views.label: Shut the outer shutter
views.read: One floating marker crosses the visible slot. The sheltered watcher has no view of the outer rail.

views.label: Open the side frame and repeat the trace
views.read: A second marker crosses beyond the first slot. Trieste’s field reports also have a viewing position and conditions. The release describes a historic dive and should keep the observer’s field of view visible.

placements.label: Send the sheltered report with its visible sector
placements.after: Ruan gives the next watch a usable inner count and draws the reach of the shutter beside it.

placements.label: Pin the wider check directly beside the old slip
placements.after: Both watch positions stay visible. The seam helps visitors tell which part was outside the original observer’s view.

question: How does the width of a window change what we can claim crossed the water?
journal: I saw one marker go by in the slot. When I opened the side frame there was another. I put the place I stood beside my report before anyone could take my narrow window for the whole harbour.
firstHint: The sheltered watcher can see part of the harbour through a slot.
thirdHint: Keep the first trace, open the side frame and look beyond the edge it hid.

title: The two-sided receipt tray
method: Give the Dhuwa petition a receipt line that leaves space for its later outcome.
request: A Cold Store docket says the claim was settled at receipt. The review keeper can separate the moment a statement reached a house from what that house recognised.

views.label: Lift the received-date leaf
views.read: Jock Nelson tabled the Dhuwa petition on 14 August 1963. That fixes a parliamentary action and a date.

views.label: Lift the separate decision leaf
views.read: The petition carried Yolŋu law and asserted objections to mining. A receipt gives no proof the decision-makers recognised ownership. The public note names the Yolŋu account and leaves the designs with their custodians.

placements.label: Clip the attributed date beside the pending outcome
placements.after: The keeper shows where the dated presentation can be checked. The outcome has a separate place with its own sources.

placements.label: Give the review desk both leaves in date order
placements.after: A second keeper can compare the two questions without reading the first date as a later acknowledgement.

question: How can a record say that a petition was received without claiming to know how it ends?
journal: I found 14 August 1963 on the Dhuwa petition’s presentation record. On the second leaf I looked for a decision. Receiving the petition let the House record an action. That date alone could never tell me how the claim was treated.
firstHint: One leaf dates what happened in Parliament. The other leaves room for what followed.
thirdHint: Lift the received-date leaf and the decision leaf separately before choosing how a visitor will follow them.

title: The protected signature sleeve
method: Trace where a public display can preserve access while its fragile evidence is housed elsewhere.
request: A visitor came for the sheet on display. The keeper has an index for the original signatures and the leaf visitors can see.

views.label: Check the exhibition leaf’s identifier
views.read: This is the Yirritja petition tabled by Arthur Calwell on 28 August 1963. Keep that date and the Yolŋu makers apart from the earlier Dhuwa presentation.

views.label: Open the care record for the signatures
views.read: The recorded care decision substituted copies for fading typed papers at the border. The archived comparison identifies what was displayed and separately where the earlier signed paper can be read.

placements.label: Lead with the public leaf and attach its exact index
placements.after: People can find the public description and take its precise identifier to the review desk for the source.

placements.label: Hang a paired care note near the keeper’s index
placements.after: The keeper leaves the original and the displayed paper on named lines so the next reader can follow each one.

question: How can people see a record while the fragile original stays safe somewhere else?
journal: I traced the Yirritja petition presented on 28 August to its own entry. The care record explained why the paper on display could differ from the earlier signed paper. I left a way to find that comparison.
firstHint: The presentation and the later preservation decision have separate records.
thirdHint: Use the Yirritja identifier first, then open the care record to see where the signed paper belongs.

title: The horizon slip beside Imani’s calendar
method: Compare a copied observation guide and what a new observer can repeat.
request: Imani needs to record two lifts of the same practice star at a low wall. The borrowed guide gives a season and the new observer needs a recorded position.

views.label: Fit the workshop’s low horizon strip
views.read: The route’s first mark meets the wall edge. A date and a position belong to this local practice observation.

views.label: Raise the strip to the clerk’s second doorway
views.read: The visible crossing now meets another mark. The 1733 Timbuktu manuscript supports a learned tradition of observing stars and seasons. The instruction travels, and a new place supplies its own conditions.

placements.label: Put the date and observation place first
placements.after: Imani keeps a local detail the next observer can repeat and leaves the manuscript’s record close to the observer’s note.

placements.label: Give the manuscript and the next observation separate leaves
placements.after: The next keeper can follow the teacher’s record and repeat the local check without merging their dates.

question: When is a copied guide enough for a new observer to repeat what someone saw?
journal: I set a star mark against the low strip and watched it meet another edge from the second doorway. The Timbuktu record tells me about a surviving manuscript copied in 1733. The two readings in my hand came from our doorways.
firstHint: A change of doorway can move the mark even while the practice sky stays still.
thirdHint: Fit the low strip, then raise it at the clerk’s doorway. Keep the local position with each reading.

title: The red proofs that go to two readers
method: Give the press a practical way to keep the exact leaf separate from an entire printing.
request: Lark has two working strips with red headings. The signed catalogue says which heading on the Library’s particular vellum copy was printed and where other headings came by hand.

views.label: Fit the leaf [129b] reference under the proof
views.read: The source strip names the Library’s exact copy and particular printed heading. With the identifier attached, a reader can follow the match.

views.label: Compare a hand-finished heading in the other slot
views.read: The paper strip looks equally red here. The catalogue describes both processes in this copy. Surface colour alone does not settle how an individual heading was added.

placements.label: Pass the matched heading with its leaf number
placements.after: Lark gives the press queue a small usable example. The copy number and leaf stay together.

placements.label: Leave the two proofs under separate process slips
placements.after: Lark opens the fuller tray for the next printer. The colour stays visible on both and each process has its own source line.

question: When does one printed page stand for a whole printing, and when does it not?
journal: I matched leaf [129b] to the reference for the Library of Congress copy. The other heading looked just as red under the press light. I needed the record to say what the colour could not tell me.
firstHint: Two headings can share a colour and have different production histories.
thirdHint: Fit the identified leaf under the proof before checking the hand-finished comparison.

title: The mark and the reader’s line
method: Use the local practice board to distinguish a visible mark from its keeper’s interpretation.
request: Leila’s sketch has a long groove and a line of marks. Visitors need to know which part they can trace and which part a trained reader would interpret.

views.label: Trace only the visible marks on the local sketch
views.read: The shape is reproducible from the same light. The dated Shang object’s catalogue describes an inscribed animal bone. The light exercise here uses its own practice sheet.

views.label: Turn over the keeper’s line of supplied context
views.read: A record of divination can tell readers about a practice and how it left a trace. A present visitor needs a distinct source before supplying a particular old reading.

placements.label: Leave a traceable outline with its practice date
placements.after: Leila moves the light sketch into a reader’s reach. The keeper’s line about the accession remains on its own slip.

placements.label: Set the catalogue description beside the lighting notes
placements.after: The workroom keeps the object’s historical account within reach and labels the visible exercise as its own comparison.

question: Where does a visible mark end and a reader's interpretation begin?
journal: I followed the light across the practice sheet. I could draw the marks again. I had to turn over the keeper’s note to learn what connected the historical inscription to divination. I left the particular old reading open.
firstHint: The workyard sketch and its supplied context can answer different requests.
thirdHint: Trace the practice marks before turning the keeper’s note. Check where seeing ends and context begins.

title: The credits that travel with a printed page
method: Find where a claim about a book’s printing should travel with a reader’s credit.
request: Mina’s practice copy has space for two role slips. The book that inspired it names people who did different work to get it to its readers.

views.label: Open the compiler’s line
views.read: Baegun’s compilation gives its text a history. The Bibliothèque nationale de France identifies its surviving July 1377 volume as a particular copy.

views.label: Lift the printing line
views.read: Seokchan and Daldam printed the volume at Heungdeoksa in Cheongju. The printing roles explain why an author line on its own would hide part of the work.

placements.label: Fit the compiler and printing lines on a single rail
placements.after: Mina’s next visitor keeps both roles in view on one pass. The accession stays below the two entries.

placements.label: Make a printer’s slip and include the shared record number
placements.after: The workshop takes the roles it needs and can follow the same exact copy number to the compiler’s line.

question: Who should get credit when a claim about a book's printing reaches a new reader?
journal: I put Baegun’s compilation beside the work of Seokchan and Daldam on the surviving 1377 volume. If I had kept only the compiler’s line, there would have been no place left on the notice for the printers.
firstHint: The work has a compiler and the surviving volume has printers.
thirdHint: Open the compiler’s line and then the printing credit. Give the July 1377 volume room on its own line.

title: Two settings for the open instrument tray
method: Pair a calibrated practice dial with the place it can describe.
request: The keeper can fit the same star marker against two plate drawings. The astronomer’s inscription and the plates leave different evidence.

views.label: Fit the first workshop plate
views.read: The first guide crosses nearer to the centre from this practice position. The wearer can keep its reading with the scale that made it.

views.label: Switch to the second plate drawing
views.read: The same sky mark crosses further out against the changed plate. The Met’s exact Yemeni instrument bears ‘Umar ibn Yusuf’s name and its 690 AH date.

placements.label: File the chosen plate and its place together
placements.after: The keeper can repeat one reading from the correct diagram. The signed instrument record stays with its own date.

placements.label: Pair the two readings under the signature reference
placements.after: The keeper sets the plates side by side with their settings named. The signed date stays separate from both readings.

question: What place can a measuring instrument describe, and where does its reading stop?
journal: I watched the same sky mark cross a different part of the second plate. I kept the plate with its reading. I could refer a visitor to the dated Yemeni instrument without pretending that our practice marks were on it.
firstHint: A reading changes when a different plate lies under the same mark.
thirdHint: Try both plates and compare the crossings before a reader takes the result.

title: The movement behind a single frame
method: Compare a still movement mark with its place in a staged sequence.
request: The theatre guide has one pause to print. A carrier saw the middle of a move, and an audience reader wants to know what makes it part of a sequence.

views.label: Slide out the one frozen stage stance
views.read: At the marked instant a foot is clear of the floor. The guide can record that instant without filling in what happened before it.

views.label: Put the marked instant between its lead and follow frames
views.read: The practice cut supplies an order and leaves its intervals unnamed. The Library of Congress item anchors the particular Sallie Gardner sequence to the Palo Alto record.

placements.label: Leave the instant first with the frame order behind it
placements.after: The stage helper can find their cue quickly and slide the frame back into its sequence.

placements.label: Put the whole sequence up along the rehearsal edge
placements.after: The audience guide can compare the moments before and after the cue without guessing an unpictured transition.

question: What can a single still image tell us about a movement, and what needs the whole sequence?
journal: I stopped the strip with a hoof clear of the floor. Running the sequence gave me an order. I still had no interval written in the gap between those views.
firstHint: A frame shows an instant and a sequence shows an order.
thirdHint: Hold the marked frame still, then run the cut and look for a time interval the strip actually supplies.

title: The source tab behind the copied doorway note
method: Try a reader’s path back to the source of a copied notice.
request: Dace has two door notices. One has the current date while the other keeps the pointer a reader can follow back to the first work sheet.

views.label: Follow the signed original pointer
views.read: The pointer leads to the keeper’s exact sheet. This copy can travel and the reader can still check the place where it began.

views.label: Open the hand-copied notice by itself
views.read: The words are present and the pointer is missing. CERN’s preserved computer gives an exact historic site to follow. Reachable copies and source pointers do different jobs.

placements.label: Put the source marker on the doorway copy
placements.after: Dace keeps a short notice usable at the door with its full route back still printed underneath.

placements.label: Leave the current and source sheets in a paired holder
placements.after: Visitors can check the doorway instructions and source side by side, with both dates close enough to compare.

question: How can a reader find the source of a notice that has been copied many times?
journal: I opened one copy and followed its pointer back to the source sheet. The other carried every word and had lost that pointer. Both could travel. Only one showed me the way back.
firstHint: Two copies can have the same words and give different access to their source.
thirdHint: Follow the pointer on one copy, then inspect what travelled on the sheet without it.

title: The star behind the door rim
method: Compare a small bright field with what the full doorway can show.
request: Imani has one narrow aperture and a wider practice frame. A mark clear through the aperture may be only part of the sketch.

views.label: Check the narrow opening
views.read: The bright point lies inside the marked rim. A second point is outside the frame. Museo Galileo’s instrument 2427 lets a reader follow a particular surviving telescope.

views.label: Swing the larger frame over the same sheet
views.read: The second point appears. Its location can be checked against the first without claiming either view showed the whole sheet.

placements.label: Give the first watcher a narrow mark with an edge
placements.after: Imani puts the bright point and the viewing limit on one slip. The next observer can repeat that observation.

placements.label: Set both frames in reach for a paired check
placements.after: The two readers keep the frame edges next to the corresponding positions. The sheet stays fixed while the frame is moved.

question: What does a narrow view show clearly, and what does it hide?
journal: I marked the point inside the narrow rim. A second point appeared in the next view. I left both positions for the person who wanted to repeat the check.
firstHint: A point can fall outside one rim and inside the next.
thirdHint: Mark the first view before widening it. Use that mark to locate the second point.

title: The lens and the wider scene
method: Check what a detailed view adds and what it leaves outside.
request: The conservator has two repairs on a practice sheet. A very close view brings one join into reach, while its position in the sheet needs a wider view.

views.label: Open the high-detail view
views.read: The join has two overlapping marks. Utrecht’s record identifies the specific Leeuwenhoek microscope. This detailed workroom drawing does not report what he observed.

views.label: Lift the sheet for its wider edges
views.read: The join is on the left quarter. At this distance the overlap is no longer visible. The local ruler helps a later visitor return to the same place.

placements.label: Pin the detail with the corner reference
placements.after: The workroom guide can bring a conservator directly back to the join. Its location stays on the small label.

placements.label: Clip the two views together
placements.after: The teaching sleeve leaves the wider context first and keeps the close detail one turn away.

question: What does a detailed view add, and what does it leave outside the frame?
journal: I could see the overlap at the join when I went close. Back at the ruler it was only a place on the left quarter. I kept its address so another pair of eyes could find it again.
firstHint: Magnifying the join helps you inspect it. The ruler helps you get back there.
thirdHint: Inspect the overlap close up and find its quarter on the wider workroom drawing.

title: The one window in the return record
method: Give an object’s voyage and its later display their own lines.
request: The station’s dock sheet combines a trip and a return in the same heading. Two readers need different dates and a place to check the record.

views.label: Open the flight leaf
views.read: The Smithsonian’s Columbia record names the Apollo 11 Command Module. Its July 1969 flight contained legs with different parts and jobs.

views.label: Open the receiving and custody leaf
views.read: This surviving vehicle has its own return and later museum identity. A display date and an earlier mission date describe different events.

placements.label: Post the flight line for the watcher
placements.after: The watcher gets a particular launch-era record and a pointer to the receiving leaf, where later custody can be checked.

placements.label: Use the receiving diagram at the station table
placements.after: The table separates the named vehicle from the voyage stages. A reader can follow either date without treating one as the other.

question: How can we keep an object's journey and its later display from being mixed up?
journal: I traced Columbia through a particular part of the July 1969 flight, then back to the object in the museum. The day someone can visit the module and the date of its journey belong to different records.
firstHint: A vehicle’s flight, return and museum record can have different dates.
thirdHint: Follow the module’s flight role in one window and the surviving object in the other.

title: The shore frame and the live harbour log
method: Keep a learning aid beside the conditions of a later observation.
request: The crew wants to put a shore lesson beside a timed harbour check. The historic Marshallese object has its own preparation and repair record.

views.label: Open the shore lesson leaf
views.read: The Smithsonian records this accession as a learning aid for preparation. Its collector’s condition note records repairs on its own line.

views.label: Move the mark to the live log
views.read: The practice watcher makes a local observation at the named bell. That slip belongs to the watcher, date and place, separate from the accession description.

placements.label: Leave a paired link beside the lesson
placements.after: Visitors can try the local diagram and follow the public accession to its own context. The live log remains separately signed.

placements.label: Put the live record on the harbour rail
placements.after: The crew gets the next observation at its working place, with a pointer back to the shore lesson for people preparing.

question: When does a learning aid help, and when do we need the live record instead?
journal: I put the practice watcher’s bell and place beside the training-aid record. The accession’s repair note belongs with that object. It cannot date the water someone saw from this shore.
firstHint: A teaching aid can prepare someone to observe. It is a different source from a dated observation.
thirdHint: Compare the accession’s use note with the watcher’s bell slip before choosing where to leave them.

title: The bench that holds a family’s record
method: Give an object’s public testimony and a viewer’s interpretation separate places.
request: A visitor wants a repair note to speak for the family. The review keeper can hold the accession and the family’s documented history separately.

views.label: Read the family line held with the object
views.read: The Hiroshima Peace Memorial Museum identifies Shinichi Tetsutani and his tricycle. The personal connection is part of this object’s history.

views.label: Open the later custody note
views.read: The museum identifies the family’s actions and later donation. A public caption can preserve that information and leave space for a visitor’s own response.

placements.label: Lead with the named account and a place to sit
placements.after: The keeper opens a quiet reading place with the family line within reach and a clear route to its recorded provenance.

placements.label: Set the custody leaf behind the family line
placements.after: Another reader can retrace where the piece went while keeping the family account visible at the front.

question: How can an object's own testimony and a viewer's interpretation each keep their place?
journal: I kept Shinichi Tetsutani’s name beside his tricycle and followed the museum’s account of the family’s later donation. I left space for a visitor’s own words. I couldn’t provide those for them.
firstHint: The name, the object and its later custody each matter to the family’s public record.
thirdHint: Read the personal connection first and then the account of the later donation. Give the next visitor room to respond.
